page.doc_title: Lunch 29 · Containers (Advanced): Azure Kubernetes Service — Interactive demo
page.title: Say what you want, and Kubernetes keeps it true
page.lede: Follow Nusantara Retail's storefront Deployment on an AKS cluster: three replicas spread over three availability zones, a node failure the cluster heals by itself, the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler at the 12.12 sale, and a rolling update with a rollback. Press ▶ Play, or step through with Next and Back.
page.svgTitle: An AKS cluster with one node in each of three availability zones runs the storefront Deployment
page.svgDesc: On the left, Rizky's kubectl talks to the AKS control plane, a board compares the Deployment's desired and actual state, and a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches CPU. In the Azure region, a LoadBalancer Service at the top sends shoppers' requests to storefront pods on three nodes, one per availability zone, and each node has room for two pods. Callouts explain each event.

steps.title: Many services, one cluster
steps.text: Dewi's team has split the shop into services, and a loyalty vendor ships a Helm chart that needs real Kubernetes. Rizky has built an AKS cluster in Southeast Asia with one node in each of three availability zones. Ibu Sari's conditions: the shop must survive a broken server and the 12.12 crowd, and nobody should have to babysit it.

steps.title: Azure runs the control plane
steps.text: AKS splits the work. Azure runs and patches the control plane: the API server that every kubectl command goes to, the etcd database, the scheduler and the controllers. On the Free tier it costs nothing but has no financially backed SLA. The nodes are virtual machines in your subscription that run the kubelet and containerd, and you pay for them by the hour.

steps.title: Declare the desired state
steps.text: Rizky applies a manifest: a Deployment named storefront with three replicas of image v1, each requesting 50 millicores of CPU and 64 MiB of memory. He never says which node to use. The API server stores this desired state in etcd. A controller compares it with reality, finds zero pods where three are wanted, and creates three pod objects.

steps.title: The scheduler spreads pods across zones
steps.text: The scheduler picks a node for each new pod. Any node has room for such small requests, and a topology spread constraint in the pod template asks for an even spread across zones, so each zone gets one pod. The kubelet on each node pulls the image and starts the container. A pod counts as ready only when its readiness probe answers.

steps.title: One address in front of moving pods
steps.text: A Service of type LoadBalancer gives the pods one stable address. AKS adds a rule and a public IP address to the cluster's Azure load balancer in the node resource group, and the Service spreads requests over the ready pods in all three zones. Pods come and go with new IP addresses, but the Service keeps track of them, so shoppers never notice.

steps.title: A node fails in zone 3
steps.text: At 14:05 the virtual machine in zone 3 stops responding. Within about a minute Kubernetes marks the node NotReady and its pod as not ready, so the Service stops sending it requests. The shop stays open on the two other pods, with less spare capacity. Look at the board: the desired state still says three. Only the actual state has changed.

steps.title: Controllers replace the lost pod
steps.text: Pods on an unreachable node get five minutes to recover. Then Kubernetes evicts them, and the controller counts two running pods where three are wanted. It creates one more, the scheduler places it on a healthy node in zone 1, and as soon as its readiness probe passes, actual state matches desired state again. Nobody had to be paged.

steps.title: The 12.12 crowd arrives
steps.text: Auto-repair has rebooted node 3, and it is Ready again, but empty: Kubernetes does not move running pods back on its own. Then the 12.12 sale starts, and the three pods average 100% of their CPU request. The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler checks every 15 seconds, compares that with its 50% target, and calculates ceil(3 × 100 ÷ 50) = 6 pods.

steps.title: The HPA adds three pods
steps.text: The HPA does not start pods itself. It raises the Deployment's desired replica count from three to six, and the controllers create three new pods. The scheduler puts them where the spread is thinnest: two on the repaired node in zone 3 and one in zone 2. They start in seconds because the nodes have room, and average CPU falls back towards the target.

steps.title: Rolling update: one pod at a time
steps.text: After the sale, the HPA waited out its five-minute stabilization window and went back to three pods. Now the team ships v2. With maxSurge 1 and maxUnavailable 0, the Deployment first adds one v2 pod. It gets no requests until its readiness probe passes; only then is one v1 pod removed, and the cycle repeats for the next pod.

steps.title: Rollout complete, shop never closed
steps.text: Three cycles later every pod runs v2, and the shop never closed: at least three ready pods stayed behind the Service the whole time. Kubernetes keeps the old ReplicaSet at zero pods, which is what makes a rollback fast. The same pattern protects you when AKS drains nodes during an upgrade, as long as you run several replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget.

steps.title: A typo in the image tag
steps.text: Next, Rizky sets a tag that does not exist: v99. The new pod cannot pull its image; its status switches between ErrImagePull and ImagePullBackOff, and kubectl describe shows the reason in its events. Because maxUnavailable is 0, no v2 pod is removed while the new one is not ready, so the rollout simply stalls and shoppers notice nothing.

steps.title: Roll back, and your turn
steps.text: kubectl rollout undo switches the Deployment back to the previous ReplicaSet, the broken pod is deleted, and the desired state is three v2 pods again. The recap: you declare what you want, Kubernetes keeps reconciling, zones and replicas absorb failures, the HPA turns load into replicas, readiness probes make updates safe, and Azure runs the control plane for you.
steps.tip: In Lab 29 you build a small AKS cluster with Azure CNI Overlay, deploy the storefront with probes, requests and limits, delete a pod and watch it come back, scale with an HPA, roll out a change, and repair an ImagePullBackOff with kubectl describe.

The new version and how to roll it out
That tag does not exist in the registry.
Node 3 is NotReady, so its pod is marked not ready and the Service skips it.
Kubernetes waits five minutes before evicting the pod, in case the node returns.
Node auto-repair: AKS reboots a node that stays NotReady for five minutes,
then reimages or redeploys it if needed. That can take up to an hour.
No room on any node? The new pods wait in Pending, and the cluster autoscaler
adds a node in a few minutes. Honest CPU and memory requests make this work.
Failed to pull image "…/storefront:v99": not found
Readiness gate: the Service sends requests to the v2 pod only after its readiness
probe passes. Then one v1 pod stops, and the next v2 pod starts.
AKS upgrades drain one node at a time. A PodDisruptionBudget with minAvailable: 2
stops a drain from evicting more storefront pods than the shop can spare.
Back to the previous ReplicaSet: three v2 pods, and the broken pod is gone.
